title: Archigenes' counter-argument against Magnus on the rapid pulse
summary: Galen recalls Archigenes' objection to Magnus that a rapid pulse comes from weakness, not strength, of the faculty, and says he refuted it in his work on causes in the pulses.
quote: the counter-argument of Archigenes against Magnus, to the effect that the rapid pulse does not arise from strength of the faculty but rather from weakness
note: The refutation is placed in the treatise on the causes in the pulses (De causis pulsuum).

title: Heraclides of Pontus on the 'breathless' condition
summary: Extreme chilling makes breathing so small that it seems gone; Galen identifies this with the state Heraclides of Pontus called 'breathless'.
quote: the condition which Heraclides of Pontus described as "breathless" is this one
note: Outside knowledge: Heraclides' lost dialogue Peri tes apnou (the woman without breath). Galen adds that neither breath nor pulse truly ceases while the animal lives.

title: Herophilus on rhythm in the pulses
summary: The rhythm of breathing (inspiration compared with expiration) can be analysed with the same theory Herophilus wrote for rhythms of the pulse.
quote: this topic will admit the same theory as that written by Herophilus concerning the rhythms in the pulses.
note: Herophilus' pulse-rhythm writings are lost; Galen is a main witness.

title: Cross-references to Galen's pulse treatises
summary: Galen says he showed in On the Use of the Pulses that breathing and the pulse give the same benefit to the heat; he also cites Causes in the Pulses (books 1-3) and On the Differences of Pulses.
quote: if indeed we did not wrongly show, in the work On the Use of the Pulses, that the same benefit comes from respiration to the heat in the heart
note: Other citations: Causes in the Pulses I (K7.768), III (K7.771), II (K7.799, K7.803-804); Differences of Pulses (K7.806-807).

title: Commentaries On the Innate Heat (lost work)
summary: Anyone puzzled by the different kinds of heat is referred to Galen's commentaries On the Innate Heat.
quote: rather to refer him to the commentaries On the Innate Heat
note: Outside knowledge: Galen's De calore innato is lost.

title: On the Movement of Muscles and commentaries On Respiration
summary: Galen refers to On the Movement of Muscles for the difference between collapse and relaxation of a part, and to his commentaries On Respiration, where the diaphragm only slackens its tension in breathing out.
quote: It has been stated at greater length in the books On the Movement of Muscles in what respect the collapse of a part differs from its letting-down and relaxation
note: K7.839-840 cites book 2 of On the Movement of Muscles for his proof that breathing is voluntary.

title: On the Causes of Respiration: diaphragm the chief organ
summary: Galen cites his books On the Causes of Respiration, where he showed the diaphragm to be the first and most important organ of breathing.
quote: which was shown by us in the books On the Causes of Respiration to be the first and most principal organ of these
note: Outside knowledge: De causis respirationis survives only as a short summary.

title: Lost works on Hippocratic anatomy and on Thucydides' plague
summary: Galen says he showed elsewhere how Hippocrates' writing differs from Thucydides', in his works on Hippocrates' anatomy and on the plague in Thucydides.
quote: in particular in those on the anatomy of Hippocrates, and not least also in those on the plague in Thucydides.
note: Outside knowledge: both works are lost; this is one of the few attestations of a Galenic work on Thucydides' plague.

title: On the Best Sect and Therapeutic Method on method of inquiry
summary: Galen refers readers to On the Best Sect and the Therapeutic Method for how to investigate such problems, and says dull readers should give up, since a small nature cannot grasp a great man's thought.
quote: It has indeed been stated both in the writings On the Best Sect and in those of the Therapeutic Method how one ought both to investigate and to discover all such things
note: Outside knowledge: Galen's own On the Best Sect is lost (the extant De optima secta is spurious).

title: Promised fourth book on Thessalus, Polybus and Euryphon
summary: Galen plans, if he has more time, a fourth book on what the other works under Hippocrates' name say about dyspnoea, including those of his son Thessalus, his son-in-law Polybus, and works thought to be by Euryphon.
quote: if ever I come to have more leisure, I shall add another, fourth book, expounding what is said about dyspnoea in the remaining works inscribed with the name of Hippocrates.
note: Polybus is called Hippocrates' son-in-law (Πολύβου τοῦ γαμβροῦ). No such fourth book is known.

title: A sophist disputes delirium breathing with Galen
summary: Galen says one of the lecturing sophists once argued with him that large, rare breathing never occurs in delirium, because it did not fit his view that breathing is a vital (involuntary) function.
quote: Indeed, one of such sophists once disputed with me about the breath's becoming large and rare in those who are delirious.
note: Personal anecdote from Galen's polemics (probably in Rome).

title: Opponent shows Galen a delirious patient and laughs
summary: A man showed Galen a delirious patient who was not breathing large and rare, mocked Hippocrates and Galen, and left without hearing that the sign holds one way only.
quote: One of such men, then, once showed us a patient who was delirious, yet breathing neither large nor
note: Galen's reply rests on the logic that large, rare breath implies delirium, but delirium does not imply large, rare breath.

title: Teachers lecturing from high thrones
summary: Galen mocks teachers who sit on high, prominent chairs in their lectures to the young, ignore clinical practice and say whatever comes to mind.
quote: But as many as, in their lecture-sessions with the young, seated upon high thrones, lofty
note: Detail of 2nd-century medical teaching. K7.828-829: such sophists 'sit indoors' and never see the sick.

title: Breathing is voluntary, moved like the legs
summary: Since breathing is a psychic (voluntary) work, an inflamed thorax breathes as an inflamed leg walks, with smaller and slower movements. Arteries cannot do this, because the pulse is a vital work.
quote: But in fact it is one of the psychic works, as has been demonstrated elsewhere; it is clear, then, that it will be moved in the same way as the legs.
note: This is the core argument of the treatise against those who held breathing to be involuntary.

title: Four diagnostic pairings of dyspnoea
summary: Large and frequent breathing shows increased need; small and rare, decreased need; large and rare is proper to delirium; small and frequent, to pain. Unevenness is a fifth sign.
quote: it was found that the large and frequent respiration indicates increase of the need, and its opposite, the small and rare, indicates diminution; and that the large and rare is peculiar to delirium
note: These pairings are the core diagnostic result of Book 1 (summary at K7.823-824).

title: Causes of small, rapid, frequent breathing
summary: Tumours of the stomach, liver, spleen or colon press on the diaphragm. In dropsy, pregnancy, over-filling, pot-belly, orthopnoea, lung growths and spinal deformity the breath is likewise small, frequent and rapid.
quote: in dropsical patients and in pregnant women and in [782] those who have been over-filled and in those with protruding bellies, the form of respiration becomes of this kind
note: Spinal deformities are named as kyphotic, lordotic and scoliotic. A narrow thorax can be present from the womb.

title: 'Rough arteries' is a mistranslation: the windpipe and bronchi
summary: Throughout the work the draft renders τραχεῖαι ἀρτηρίαι as 'rough arteries'. In Galen the phrase means the windpipe and its branches in the lung, the air passages.
quote: when viscous and thick humours collect in the rough arteries in the lung
note: Known mis-rendering, recorded once for the whole work; read 'bronchi/air-passages' wherever 'rough arteries' appears. The 'smooth arteries' (K7.801) are ordinary arteries.

title: Signs of weak respiratory faculty: nostrils, shoulder muscles, collapse
summary: When the breathing faculty is weak and chilled, the wings of the nose move, the muscles about the shoulder-blades work, and the thorax collapses all at once on breathing out.
quote: he will have the movement of the wings of the nose, and the activity of all the muscles about the shoulder-blades, and the sudden collapse of the thorax.
note: Early description of nasal flaring and use of the accessory muscles as signs of failing breathing.

title: Delirious patients forget the chamber-pot
summary: Galen has seen many delirious patients ask for a chamber-pot and then hold it without urinating, or sit down to defecate and forget, until reminded. Breathing in delirium is likewise slow but large.
quote: we know of very many who asked for a chamber-pot, but when it was given no longer urinated, but held it idly in their two hands
note: Clinical observation used to explain why breathing in delirium is large and rare.

title: Dialectic: the sign converts only one way
summary: 'If he breathes large and rare, he is delirious' is not the same as 'if he is delirious, he breathes large and rare'. The two statements do not convert, they only invert; large, rare breath is a property of delirium, not inseparable from it.
quote: For these do not convert (ἀντιστρέφειν) with one another, but only invert (ἀναστρέφειν).
note: The Greek has the finite verbs ἀντιστρέφει/ἀναστρέφει. Galen defends the dialectic his opponents despise, with an Olympic-training analogy.

title: The Epidemics are notes, not finished treatises
summary: Hippocrates wrote about dyspnoea both in his treatises and in his notes; most or all of the Epidemics should be counted as notes (hypomnemata).
quote: For most of the Epidemics, if indeed not all of them, one would rightly consider to be notes.

title: Authorship of the seven Epidemics books
summary: Book 7 is plainly spurious and later. Book 5 is by the younger Hippocrates, son of Draco. Books 2, 4 and 6 are variously given to Hippocrates' son or to Hippocrates himself as notes; only books 1 and 3 are agreed to be by the great Hippocrates.
quote: the fifth is not by the great Hippocrates, the son of Heraclides, but by the younger one, the son of Draco
note: Key testimony on how the Hippocratic corpus was judged in antiquity.

title: Thessalus and 'the things from the small tablet'
summary: Some think five Epidemics books were written by Thessalus and two by the great Hippocrates. Hence the title 'from the small tablet', because Thessalus gathered everything his father had written so that nothing would be lost.
quote: to have been entitled "the things from the small tablet", evidently because Thessalus was eager to gather into one place everything that his father happened to have written
note: An otherwise rare title. Galen says these critics have grasped the character of the books most accurately.

title: Regimen in Acute Diseases, also called Against the Cnidian Sentences
summary: The Prognostic, Aphorisms, Airs Waters Places, and Regimen in Acute Diseases (titled by some Against the Cnidian Sentences) are believed genuine. Other works are assigned to Euryphon, Thessalus and Polybus.
quote: On Regimen in Acute Diseases, which some entitle Against the Cnidian Sentences, are not unreasonably believed to be writings of Hippocrates himself.
note: Outside knowledge: the Cnidian Sentences are a lost work of the Cnidian school (associated with Euryphon).

title: Regimen in Acute Diseases titled On Ptisan; its ending disputed
summary: Some call Regimen in Acute Diseases 'On Ptisan'. No critic has denied it to Hippocrates, but many remove the final part after the section on baths.
quote: For the parts at the end, those after the use of the bath, many remove, but the parts up to that point all preserve.
note: Ancient testimony that the appendix (Acut. Spur.) was regarded as not genuine.

title: Erasistratus' definition of phlegmone
summary: In Erasistratus and the later physicians 'phlegmone' means a hard, hot, painful swelling, whereas the ancients used the word for burning heat (phlogosis).
quote: "inflammation" (phlegmone) being understood here as the hard, hot and painful swelling, as Erasistratus is accustomed to call it and all the more recent physicians
note: K7.910-911 adds that nearly everyone before Erasistratus called phlogosis 'phlegmone'.

title: Hippocrates writes as craftsman, Thucydides as layman
summary: Thucydides records everything laymen notice about the sick. Hippocrates leaves out the obvious and records the technical details that even good physicians miss.
quote: For Thucydides wrote the things that happened to the sick as a layman for laymen, but Hippocrates as a craftsman for craftsmen.
note: Galen corrects 'the ancients' who thought Hippocrates writes down everything, as Thucydides does (K7.850).

title: Galen cites book and case number; commentators tamper
summary: Galen gives the book and position of each patient so readers can check him. He accuses many commentators of altering citations and hiding their sources.
quote: or suspect that we too are tampering in our citations (παραγράφοντας), which indeed many of the commentators have done.
note: Galen's citation practice: book, number counted from the start or from the constitution, places and headings.

title: Philiscus (Epidemics I, case 1): breath rare and large
summary: Philiscus, the first patient after the three constitutions in Epidemics I, breathed throughout 'as of one recollecting himself, rare and large'. He was delirious, and his spleen was swollen but not painful.
quote: For in this man, he says, the breath throughout was, as of one recollecting himself, rare and large.
note: K7.871-872: the swollen spleen was neither painful nor pressing on the diaphragm, so delirium set the form of breathing.

title: Wife of Dromeades: rigor after childbirth, delirium, convulsion
summary: After childbirth the wife of Dromeades had a rigor on day 2, then delirium and rare, large breathing. Galen later notes she died seized by convulsion, matching the 'drawn up' (uneven) breath.
quote: "The wife of Dromeades," he says, "having given birth, and all the other things having gone according to reason, being on the second day, a rigor seized her."
note: The Greek name form is Δρομάδεω (Dromades). For the death by convulsion see K7.931-932.

title: Count of patients in Epidemics I and III
summary: Galen counts sixteen patients in Epidemics I, with rare, large breathing mentioned four times. Later he counts fourteen patients in book I, and in book III twelve before and sixteen after the pestilential constitution.
quote: In the first book of the Epidemics, then, Hippocrates, having described sixteen patients in all, is seen making mention of rare and large breathing four times.
note: Inconsistency: K7.879-880 says 'These fourteen patients' (τεσσαρεσκαίδεκα ἄῤῥωστοι) from book I, perhaps counting only those after Philiscus and Silenus. Worth checking against the Greek.

title: Pythion (Epidemics III): delirious but breath thin
summary: Pythion, third after the pestilential constitution in Epidemics III, was delirious, yet his breath was 'thin and diminished' and short. Galen explains this by belly pain and chilling overriding the delirium.
quote: "Eighth day: in the morning he slept a little, but suddenly chilling, loss of voice, breath thin and diminished; late he grew warm again; he was deranged."
note: K7.867-869 gives the pain ('heaviness with pain' in the belly) and repeated coldness of the extremities.

title: Wife of Dealces in Thasos, on the Leion
summary: Sick from grief with an acute shivering fever, she wrapped herself up, picked at hairs and swung between tears and laughter. Her breathing was mostly rare and large, sometimes short, and she died on day 21.
quote: 'In Thasos the wife of Dealces, who lay sick on the Leion, was seized by an acute fever with shivering, arising from grief
note: Galen reads her drinking only when reminded, the parched skin and the drinks passing straight through as signs of the innate heat dying out (K7.866-867).

title: Young man in Meliboea: quiet delirium to madness
summary: The young man in Meliboea became quietly delirious on day 10, talked much nonsense on day 14 and went mad on day 20. His orderly, silent character made the delirium more serious, and his breath stayed large and rare.
quote: "on the tenth of the days he became delirious quietly, on the fourteenth he talked much nonsense, on the twentieth he went mad," he says.
note: His hypochondrium was 'somewhat slack' (ὑπολάπαρος, 'somewhat empty', K7.863-864), so it did not override the delirium.

title: Anaxion: pleurisy described by its symptoms
summary: Anaxion had acute fever, constant right-side pain and a dry cough, then delirium on day 6 and dyspnoea on day 7. Galen explains why Hippocrates lists the symptoms rather than writing 'pleuritic'.
quote: let us mention Anaxion, whom, as he himself says, an acute fever seized; continuous pain of the right side; he coughed dry, and did not spit during the first days.
note: Galen says four things are necessary in pleurisy: side pain, fever, dyspnoea and cough (K7.856-857, πλευριτικοῖς).

title: 'Hippocrates used baths over the head' in Meton's case
summary: The draft says Hippocrates 'used baths over the head', followed by a quotation about repeated nosebleeds after the crisis. The Greek says this literally, but it fits the argument poorly.
quote: whence Hippocrates used baths over the head, saying, 'he bled from the nose often after the crisis.'
note: The Greek may be corrupt, or a fragment of the Epidemics lemma may be misplaced. Check against Epid. I (Meton) and the critical apparatus.

title: Criton: great-toe pain, raving, death on day 2
summary: A man going about his normal business got violent pain in his great toe, became slightly warm on day 1, raved, and died on day 2. Galen thinks Hippocrates could not have watched his breathing.
quote: a man who was going about and doing his customary activities, and then had violent pain in the great toe of his foot, should on the first day become slightly warmed and on the next day die.
note: The patient is named Criton at K7.875-876.

title: 'Elevated' breath means small, not large
summary: Galen rejects those who take 'elevated' (meteoron) to mean large breath that lifts the thorax; for him it is the small, shallow breath of pain or cynanche.
quote: those are mistaken who suppose that 'elevated' (μετέωρον) is said in place of 'great', on the ground that it lifts up the thorax
note: Lexical dispute over a Hippocratic term.

title: Copyist's error in Epidemics II preserved in all copies
summary: The division of dyspnoeas in Epidemics II lacks the fourth pairing that Epidemics VI has. Galen blames an ancient copyist: the faulty book was published, and earlier scholars only noted the gap without daring to fix it.
quote: Rather, one of the ancient copyists erred; then the book, being in this condition, had already been published, and this very error was understandably preserved down to the present day
note: Galen's textual-critical principles: rewriting the text is rash, small additions are allowed (K7.893-894). A copyist who removes phrases makes himself 'a corrector of Hippocrates, not a servant'.

title: Rejected reading 'as those who breathe in cold upon hot'
summary: Some editors join 'hot, cold' to the previous phrase and read 'as those who breathe in cold upon hot'. Galen rejects this as senseless and keeps hot and cold breath as a separate pair of dyspnoeas.
quote: writing not 'cold and hot', as it has now been stated, but joining these words to what precedes and reading thus: 'as in those who breathe in cold upon hot'
note: A variant reading of Epid. VI (and II) recorded only by Galen.

title: Prognostic: cold breath from nose and mouth is deadly
summary: Galen quotes the Prognostic on three dyspnoeas: frequent breath signals pain or inflammation above the diaphragm, large and slow breath signals delirium, and cold breath from the nose and mouth is already very deadly.
quote: and breathed out cold [902] from the nostrils and the mouth it is already exceedingly deadly.
note: K7.928-929: chilled respiratory organs mean death because the heart, source of the innate heat, lies there.

title: On Joints: kyphosis above the diaphragm and wheezing
summary: Galen quotes On Joints: people with a hump above the diaphragm grow a pointed chest, are short of breath and wheezing, and often have hard, unripe lung growths.
quote: and they themselves become dyspnoeic and wheezing (kerchnōdeis); for the cavities that receive and send forth the breath have less straightness of direction.
note: Galen equates κέρχνος (On Joints) with ῥέγχος (Regimen in Acute Diseases).

title: Regimen in Acute Diseases: ptisan timing in pleurisy
summary: Galen quotes Hippocrates: if side pain persists despite hot applications and the sputum is not coming up, relieve the pain by softening the belly or bleeding before giving ptisan, or the patients die quickly.
quote: either by softening the belly or by cutting a vein, whichever of the two of these is indicated, and yet gives the ptisans to those in such a condition, the deaths of such patients come quickly.
note: Also: giving gruel before clearing the bowels makes the breath more frequent (K7.914, K7.924-925).

title: The ancients called such patients 'struck' (blētoi)
summary: Quoting Regimen in Acute Diseases: the ancients called pleuritics who died suffocated 'struck', partly because after death the side is found livid, as if from a blow.
quote: The ancients very much called such persons 'struck' (blētoi), chiefly for this reason, and not least because, when they have died, the side is found livid, somewhat like a blow.
note: Hippocrates reporting earlier usage. The same passage has sputum held 'in the bronchi of the lung' (βρόγχοισι).

title: Holding the breath cures yawning and hiccups
summary: Holding the breath as long as possible ('retention of breath') cures continuous yawning, for the same reason it cures hiccups. Athletes also hold the breath after exercise to force moisture and vapour out of the pores.
quote: For holding the respiration for as long as possible, which is called retention of breath, will cure yawnings by the same reasoning by which it cures hiccups.
note: The athletes' practice is in the same unit (σύμπαντες οἱ ἀθληταὶ).

title: Provoking anger to rouse innate heat
summary: Galen notes that Epidemics II advises cultivating a sharp temper to restore colour and spread the humours, since anger stirs the innate heat. He would use it now and then, in moderation, for the chilled, pale and lean.
quote: in the second book of the Epidemics too he advised making it a practice to induce sharpness of temper, both for the sake of the recovery of complexion and for the sake of the diffusion of the humours
note: Galen compares it to measured exercise. Frequent ('short') breathing heats and fans chilled parts.

title: Hysterical suffocation and apnoeas in barren women
summary: Hysterical suffocation and all the apnoeas often affect women, especially the barren, and rarely men. The innate heat is smothered by cold matter like a flame choked by wet wood, and can be rekindled.
quote: Among these belong also the so-called hysterical suffocation and in general all the apnoeas, which befall women continually, and especially those who are barren, but rarely on occasion men as well.
note: K7.958-959 adds childless women who are not properly purged and long-term widows.

title: Detecting breath in apnoea: finger, hair, wool
summary: In apparent apnoea the breath is only very small and slow. It can be detected by holding a finger before the nose, or by hanging a hair or fine carded wool there and watching it move.
quote: And if one also hangs a hair before it, or a fine piece of wool, thoroughly carded out, one will see these too being stirred.
note: Bedside test for faint breathing.

title: The man from the mines
summary: Epidemics IV: a man from the mines had a tense right hypochondrium, a large spleen, a tense and hard belly, and was 'full of pneuma' and colourless. Galen says the term could mean short of breath or bloated.
quote: 'The man from the mines: right hypochondrium tense, spleen large, belly tense, somewhat hard, full of pneuma, colourless.'
note: Social detail: a mine worker as a patient.

title: Newly bought female house-slave as patient
summary: Epidemics IV records a newly bought female house-slave with a large, not very painful hardness on her right side, who was 'not very dyspnoeic'.
quote: "For the female house-slave, whom I saw when she was newly bought, [955] in whom the hardening (sklerysma) in the right parts was large, not very painful"
note: Evidence that physicians examined slaves, possibly at the time of purchase.

title: Hipposthenes in Larissa: wrestling fall mistaken for peripneumonia
summary: Hipposthenes fell on his back on hard ground while wrestling, with his opponent landing on him. He bathed in cold water, then had fever, a dry cough, pain on coughing and frequent breathing. Physicians thought it peripneumonia, but he had no stertor.
quote: 'In Larissa, Hipposthenes seemed to the physicians to be gripped by peripneumonia; but it was not so at all. The beginning: while wrestling he fell on his back on hard ground, and [his opponent] fell upon him;
note: Epidemics V, case 14.

title: Daughter of Agisis: lifted a heavy load after childbirth
summary: Short of breath since girlhood, after childbirth she carelessly lifted a great weight, felt a noise in her chest, then had asthma, pain in the right hip and frothy sputum. Galen infers an old lung growth had burst.
quote: being in distress not long after childbirth, she carelessly lifted a great weight, and immediately there seemed to be a noise in her chest; on the following day she had asthma
note: Epidemics VI. Galen uses the case to separate frequent breathing from asthma.

title: Galen saw five non-axillary shoulder dislocations
summary: Hippocrates says he saw the humerus dislocate only into the armpit. Galen says he has seen other dislocations five times, once in Asia and four times in Rome.
quote: we ourselves too have seen them five times up to now, once in Asia, and four times in Rome.
note: The unit's checks failed, but the Greek confirms the figures (πεντάκις... ἐν Ῥώμῃ δὲ τετράκις).

title: Galen's student years in Smyrna
summary: Galen first saw a forward shoulder dislocation while still studying under his teachers in Smyrna, a city he says is many times larger than Hippocrates' home town.
quote: In our Asia I first beheld such a dislocation while still being educated under the teachers there, in Smyrna.
note: Biographical: confirms Galen's study at Smyrna (outside knowledge: under Pelops).

title: Galen lived in Rome after his thirtieth year
summary: Galen says that after his thirtieth year he lived in Rome, a city so crowded that it explains how often he met rare injuries.
quote: after my thirtieth year I lived in Rome, a city possessing so great a multitude of human beings
note: Chronological datum for Galen's arrival in Rome (outside knowledge: c. AD 162).

title: Polemon the rhetor: Rome an epitome of the world
summary: Galen cites the praise given to Polemon the rhetor for calling Rome an epitome of the inhabited world.
quote: Polemon the rhetor is praised for having called it an epitome of the inhabited world.
note: Outside knowledge: Antonius Polemon of Laodicea, 2nd-century sophist; the saying is otherwise known mainly from Athenaeus.

title: Physicians brought Galen their unusual cases
summary: Galen says all the physicians in Rome showed him unexpected cases for consultation, so such dislocations could not escape him.
quote: since all the physicians seem (ἐοικέναι) to show me the unexpected cases [347] for the sake of consultation (συμβολῆς)
note: ἐοικέναι ('seem') is odd here; probably read εἰωθέναι ('are accustomed'). The draft keeps the transmitted word.

title: Ostia: Galen's network of physician friends
summary: Not even at the harbour and the nearby city of Ostia could such a case escape Galen, because all the physicians practising there were his friends.
quote: not even at the harbour and the city near it which they call Ostia, because all those practising medicine in those districts too were friends
note: Evidence of Galen's professional network around Rome and Portus/Ostia.

title: Hippocrates' towns smaller than one Roman street-block
summary: The cities where Hippocrates spent most of his time had no more inhabitants than one street-block of Rome, which explains why Galen saw more rare dislocations.
quote: The cities, however, which Hippocrates mentioned as having spent the greater part of his time in did not have more inhabitants than a single street-block of those in Rome.
note: ἄμφοδον: a city block or district.

title: Causes: wrestling schools and badly trained physicians
summary: Galen blames falls in the wrestling schools and physicians who lever joints clumsily. Today's physicians learned briefly or not at all, while wrestling holds now twist limbs in many ways.
quote: but those of today have either not learned at all or have learned in an altogether short time. Then too, in the practice of wrestling-holds there has been an astonishing advance
note: Polemic on contemporary medical training.

title: Axillary dislocations wedged forward by unskilled levering
summary: Two of Galen's patients said the shoulder had first gone into the armpit, but physicians levered it clumsily and wedged the joint among the muscles.
quote: For two of those I saw said that the dislocation had occurred into the armpit, but that, when the physicians levered it unskilfully, the joint had been wedged
note: Doctor-caused injury.

title: Reduction of a forward dislocation with strap counter-extension
summary: At the Smyrna wrestling school, a wrestler's arm spread out by his opponent threw the joint forward, and Galen reduced it on the spot. With the patient on his back, an assistant seated behind pulled a broad strap round the armpit over a pad. Galen pushed the head past the constricting muscles, then relaxed the extension so the muscles drew it into the socket.
quote: Having laid the patient down on his back, we made the counter-extension similar to that performed by means of the heel, seating someone behind him and throwing a broad strap around the armpit
note: The general aims are counter-extension, levering and replacement, but the levering differs from that for an axillary dislocation.

title: Equal-tension nooses and the Hippocratic bench
summary: Extension can be done by hand, by the heel, or by a noose of equal tension such as the double karchesios knot or one made of two diantees. For a chronic dislocation Galen needed the Hippocratic bench.
quote: The noose must be of equal tension, such as is the double karchesios knot and the one made of two diantees (διαντέων).
note: Technical knot names; διαντέων is obscure (compare the knots in Oribasius' Book 48/49 on nooses).

title: Plough-oxen suffer most in winter (Homer)
summary: Homer rightly saw that oxen suffer most of all grazing animals in winter, and plough-oxen most of all, because they work through the winter and cannot crop short grass.
quote: For Homer had well observed that of all grazing beasts oxen suffer most at this season, and of oxen the plough-oxen, because they work during the winter.
note: Lemma text (Hippocrates), not Galen's own words; Galen notes Homer's 'welcome spring' line for the crumple-horned oxen (K18a.356-357).

title: Bandaging after shoulder reduction: cerate, compresses, wool pad
summary: Treat with cerate, compresses and many linen bandages; fill the armpit with a roll of soft clean wool as a counter-support; keep the upper arm inclined upward; then bind the arm to the side with a band round the body.
quote: Such patients, then, one must treat [362] with cerate and compresses and many linen bandages, binding them underneath. And one should place in the armpit soft, clean wool rolled up together
note: Hippocratic lemma (De articulis).

title: Corrupt phrase in bandaging lemma: οἵη ἑκάστῳ εἴη χωρίου
summary: The draft marks the phrase οἵη ἑκάστῳ εἴη χωρίου as corrupt and guesses the sense 'farthest from the place the head slipped into'.
quote: for in this way it would be (as it seems, 'farthest' from—the text οἵη ἑκάστῳ εἴη χωρίου is corrupt) the place into which the head of the shoulder slipped.
note: Compare the Hippocratic text of De articulis 11 (ἑκαστάτω, 'farthest'), which supports the draft's guess.

title: Thinness from famine, siege or grief makes flesh moister
summary: People thinned by famine, siege, grief or loss of appetite do not get dry flesh, as those reduced by the art do. Their flesh partly melts and becomes moister and mucous.
quote: Those who, through famine or through siege or grief or distress or loss of appetite, taking in nourishment insufficiently, have been made thin
note: Social detail: siege starvation as a medical category.

title: Rubbing the shoulder in every direction
summary: Rub gently with soft hands, top to bottom and bottom to top, obliquely, in circles and across, to soften all the muscle fibres. Galen notes that 'anatripsis' covers every kind of rubbing, not only upward strokes.
quote: It must be performed in many forms, the hands being carried around from above downward and from below upward
note: Galen defines rubbing more fully elsewhere.

title: Commentaries on In the Surgery and the treatise on hygiene
summary: Galen says rubbing is discussed in his commentaries on the Hippocratic In the Surgery and most fully in his treatise on hygiene.
quote: matters about which it has been spoken both in [366] the commentaries on that book and, indeed, most completely in the treatise on hygiene.
note: The hygiene work is De sanitate tuenda; the In the Surgery commentary is In Hipp. de officina medici.

title: Recurrent shoulder dislocation ends athletic and military careers
summary: Hippocrates says many men, otherwise capable, have been kept from athletic contests by a shoulder that keeps dislocating, and many became useless in war and died because of it.
quote: For many men have already been prevented from athletic contest by this misfortune, though in all other respects fully capable, and many have become useless in matters of war
note: Hippocratic lemma; the unit's checks failed, but the Greek matches.

title: Physicians cauterise recurrent dislocations in the wrong places
summary: Many physicians burn the top of the shoulder, the front or behind. Since the humerus dislocates downward, these burns rather encourage the dislocation by closing the space above.
quote: For many physicians have already cauterised dislocating shoulders both at the epomis and in front, where the head of the humerus bulges out, and a little behind the epomis.
note: Hippocratic polemic, endorsed by Galen.

title: Armpit cautery for recurrent dislocation
summary: Pinch up the armpit skin along the line the humerus head slips out, and burn right through it from side to side with a red-hot iron.
quote: having taken hold of the skin at the armpit with the fingers, draw it away, most of all along the very line in which the head of the humerus dislocates.
note: The unit's checks failed; the Greek supports the rendering.

title: Cautery irons: elongated, not thick or 'bald'
summary: Use glowing irons that are elongated, not thick or rounded at the tip, so they pass through quickly and leave small eschars. Galen identifies 'bald' irons with the pyrenes (diapyrina) and spathomelai.
quote: One must cauterize such parts with irons that are not thick, nor too bald, but elongated; for they pass through more quickly
note: Instrument names. The Greek has σπαθομίλαι for 'spathomelai'.

title: Spurious 'On the Whole Constitution of the Glands'
summary: Hippocrates promised a treatise on the glands, but none survives. A later Hippocratean wrote a little book under that title, far below Hippocrates in style and thought, unknown to earlier physicians and to the compilers of the catalogues (pinakes).
quote: one of the more recent Hippocrateans wrote a small little book, giving it the title Hippocrates' On the Whole Constitution of the Glands
note: Outside knowledge: the extant Hippocratic De glandulis may be this book. The pinakes reference suggests Alexandrian library catalogues.

title: Hippocratic 'cords' (tonoi) are nerves
summary: The 'most critical cords' under the armpit are the nerves. Galen mocks recent physicians who limit the word to the paired nerves from the brain on the strength of an Epidemics passage.
quote: He says that beneath the part under the armpit lie critical cords, naming the nerves in this way.
note: The nerves to the hand come from the spinal cord in the neck (K18a.380-381).

title: Menander's play The Self-Punisher cited for grammar
summary: To show that the middle τιμωρούμενος means 'punishing', Galen cites the title of Menander's play Heauton timoroumenos, along with a line of Euripides' Orestes.
quote: thus at any rate the play of Menander is entitled Heauton timoroumenos (The Self-Punisher)
note: Outside knowledge: Menander's play is lost (Terence adapted it). The Euripides line is quoted in K18a.384 ('Doing unholy deeds, yet taking vengeance for my father').

title: Galen's tally: four cases at the shoulder-vein region, one outside
summary: The head of the humerus lodged four times in the region of the shoulder vein, where the pectoral and deltoid meet, and once outside the middle region.
quote: where the two muscles come together, the great one from the sternum and the one named deltoid, has been seen by us four times to receive the dislocation
note: ὠμιαία φλέψ: the cephalic vein.

title: Most copies wrongly read 'posterior eschar'
summary: Galen says most copies wrongly read 'and again another posterior eschar', because the site is on the outer side of the joint, not behind it.
quote: But in most of the copies the wording is not correctly written thus, 'and again another posterior eschar'; for this place is not behind the articulation, but on the outside.
note: Galen's evidence on the manuscripts of De articulis.

title: Galiankones: weasel-armed from birth
summary: People born 'galiankones' (short upper arms) result from a dislocation in the womb or from deep suppuration at the humeral head in infancy. Galen leaves open whether the name comes from weasels (γαλαῖ).
quote: Whether the galiankones were so named from their resemblance to weasels (γαλαῖ) or from something else, one must leave it to those who busy themselves with such matters to investigate carefully.
note: Congenital or early-acquired shortening of the humerus.

title: Tasks possible with an unreduced shoulder
summary: Adults with an unreduced dislocated shoulder cannot lift the elbow sideways, but can still draw a drill or saw, hew with an axe and dig, provided the elbow is not raised high.
quote: for they could draw a drill (ἀρίς) and a saw, and could hew with an axe and dig, provided they do not raise the elbow very much upward
note: Hippocratic lemma; manual-labour detail.

title: Acromion avulsion mistaken for dislocation
summary: When the acromion (acromioclavicular junction) is torn away, the shoulder top looks hollow. Physicians mistake it for a dislocation and do harm trying to reduce it; the right treatment is bandaging with compresses over the projecting bone.
quote: I know, then, many physicians, not bad in other respects, who have already done much harm in trying to reduce such shoulders, supposing them to have been dislocated in this way
note: Hippocratic lemma; it sets up Galen's account of his own injury.

title: Galen's own injury in the palaestra at age 34
summary: Galen tore away his own acromion (acromioclavicular separation) while wrestling in his thirty-fifth year. He adds that he could not cure any other grown man the same way, because none could bear the bandaging.
quote: for it befell me to suffer thus in the wrestling-school when I was in my thirty-fifth year
note: Greek: ἔτος ἄγοντι ε΄ καὶ λ΄ (in his 35th year, i.e. aged 34; outside knowledge: c. AD 163, in Rome).

title: Forty days of tight bandaging closed a three-finger gap
summary: Galen bore forcing bandages for forty days, feeling the clavicle throb as it bent. It came back so close to the humerus that people now doubt it was ever torn away, though the gap had been three fingers wide. The arm wasted and then recovered.
quote: I endured this for up to forty days, during which the clavicle was brought so close to the head of the humerus that those who see it now disbelieve that it was ever torn away
note: Galen explains that young, porous bones bend like green wood. The upper arm and forearm atrophied and recovered after the bandages came off.

title: Warm-oil affusion day and night in the Dog-days
summary: The region felt cold, so Galen had warm oil poured over it day and night while he lay naked on a hide. A basin caught the run-off, which was reheated in a cauldron over a fire. When they stopped, his neck muscles tightened, threatening spasm.
quote: I was compelled [402] throughout the whole day and night to pour warm oil over it, a hide having been spread beneath my whole body, for I lay naked upon it
note: Season: the burning heat under the Dog-star (τῶν ὑπὸ κύνα καυμάτων).

title: The trainer who misdiagnosed Galen's shoulder
summary: The wrestling trainer (paidotribes) took the low shoulder for a dislocation into the armpit and kept extending and levering. Galen felt the armpit with the fingers of his good hand, found nothing out of place, and ordered them to stop.
quote: the trainer, seeing that the epomis was low and that the humerus had slipped into the armpit, both extended it and set about levering it
note: Galen diagnosed his own injury by self-palpation.

title: A distinguished bystander stops the extension
summary: The others thought Galen was going soft from the pain and kept pulling, which could have torn the muscle. By chance a distinguished man saw this was not weakness, sent them away and asked Galen what to do.
quote: had not by chance another man, a distinguished one, who saw well that I would never have restrained them from the extension out of softness, dismissed those men
note: The man is unnamed.

title: Galen's self-treatment: oil, linen, wool and a bath
summary: Galen asked for oil, a linen bandage and wool, went to the bath, and lay in the tub with much oil poured over him while the supplies were fetched. He says most people would rather keep the deformity than suffer forty days of bandaging.
quote: I needed oil and [404] linen bandage and wool; I myself went off to the bath and, having a great deal of oil poured over me, I lingered in the basin as long as was possible
note: Galen thinks the clavicle cannot be bent back in fewer than forty days.

title: Lead weight bandaged onto a broken clavicle
summary: Some have devised the refinement of binding on a heavy piece of lead to press down the projecting fragment. Hippocrates judges this useless, since the projecting part cannot be pushed down that way.
quote: There are indeed some who have already devised the refinement of binding on in addition a heavy piece of lead, so as to force down the projecting part.
note: Hippocratic lemma reporting a rival technique.

title: Girdle and perineal bandaging for clavicle fracture rejected
summary: Some tie a girdle round the patient and run the bandage from it over the clavicle, or round the perineum, seat and spine. These seem sound in theory but slip when the patient moves and are troublesome.
quote: carrying the bandage in a circle round the perineum and alongside the seat itself and along the spine, in this way they compress the fracture.
note: Hippocratic lemma. Galen adds that porous bones form callus quickly.

title: Simonides fragment for στενυγρός ('narrow')
summary: To show that στενυγρός simply means 'narrow', Galen quotes Simonides on a man meeting a leopard alone on a narrow path in shadowy mountains. Part of the verse is corrupt.
quote: This is also quite clear from what Simonides said, the words running roughly thus: 'Not yet did any man thus in the shadowy mountains,
note: The draft marks λέγονται δὶς ἐν as corrupt (perhaps 'a lion'). A poetic fragment preserved here; check against the Simonides editions (PMG).

title: Hippocrates and Xenophon mix rare words into plain style
summary: Like Xenophon, Hippocrates writes in ordinary language but inserts figurative and rare words, more often than Xenophon does, such as kinklismos and ploōdēs ('floating', i.e. unsupported).
quote: Hippocrates is accustomed to use figurative (tropical) and glossematic words for his notions, even though he employs the ordinary (civil) mode of expression; Xenophon has undergone something similar to this.
note: Ancient stylistic comparison.

title: Clavicle fracture: fourteen days' rest suffice
summary: Customary bandaging with the right posture heals it quickly. Lying down helps greatly; fourteen days are enough if the patient keeps still, and twenty are very many. 'Customary' bandaging is like an unwritten law.
quote: yet for the man to lie down makes a great difference, and fourteen days are sufficient, if he keeps still, and twenty are very many.
note: Hippocratic lemma; Galen adds the 'unwritten law' (ἄγραφον) gloss.

title: Commentaries on On Fractures
summary: Galen refers to his commentaries on On Fractures, where fracture-type (circular) bandaging is treated, as opposed to the distributive bandaging of the present book.
quote: For it has been shown by me also through the commentaries on that book, and it has been recalled even now
note: Galen's commentary on De fracturis is extant.

title: Authorship: Polybus; title 'On the Nature of Man and Regimen'
summary: Galen treats Regimen in Health as a separate book from On the Nature of Man. With the interpolated material between them removed, some titled the whole 'On the Nature of Man and Regimen'. He accepts the common attribution to Polybus.
quote: Let it be assumed to be the work of Polybus, as has seemed right to many.
note: Galen calls On the Nature of Man faultless, the interpolated part entirely faulty, and Regimen in Health mostly faultless.

title: Galen read the book with his teachers
summary: Galen admits that when he read this book with his teachers he never asked whom it calls 'private persons'; earlier commentators also left the question unexamined.
quote: Nor indeed did I myself ever inquire into it during the reading of the book with my teachers.
note: Evidence of how Hippocratic texts were read with teachers in Galen's training.

title: Who are the 'private persons' (idiōtai)?
summary: Galen argues that the regimen is not for everyone. It excludes athletes, whose diet is fixed to bread and meat, and soldiers, travellers and men in public life; it is for those 'minding their own affairs'.
quote: he seemed to me to separate the athletes outright from the rest of human beings, since those men have one regimen, defined in bread and the eating of meats.
note: K15.176-177 names the ἰδιοπραγοῦντες.

title: Soldiers, travellers and the 'circumstantial life'
summary: People at war, travelling or fighting must eat whatever is at hand, as must those on hurried journeys, in civic business, or living the so-called 'circumstantial' life.
quote: and in general for those who are engaged in civic occupations, or in what is called the 'circumstantial' life (περιστατικὸς βίος).
note: The Greek has the dative; the draft gives the nominative in brackets.

title: Winter regimen: much food, little and strong wine, roasts
summary: In winter eat as much and drink as little as possible: wine as unmixed as possible, bread, all dishes roasted, few vegetables, to keep the body warm and dry.
quote: The drink should be wine as unmixed as possible; the foods should be bread, and the dishes all roasted.
note: Galen: 'as much as possible' means relative to the other seasons, not to capacity (K15.178).

title: Heating and drying foods: lentil, cabbage, game, salted meat
summary: As further examples of warming, drying foods, Galen adds the lentil among pulses, cabbage among vegetables, and among meats those of wild animals and salted meats.
quote: You, however, will select also among the pulses those that heat and dry, such as the lentil; and also among the vegetables those that possess this power, such as the cabbage

title: On the Faculties of Foodstuffs in three books
summary: Galen says the whole range of foods is set out item by item in his three books On the Faculties of Foodstuffs.
quote: The whole material of foodstuffs, taken item by item, is set out in three treatises bearing this title: On the Faculties of Foodstuffs.
note: De alimentorum facultatibus (extant, 3 books).

title: Germans called 'yellow' but are really red
summary: Galen says writers who use colour words loosely confuse the teaching; for example, some call the Germans yellow (xanthoi), though strictly they are red.
quote: Thus, at any rate, some call the Germans yellow, although they are not yellow, if one wishes to name them accurately, but red.
note: Ethnographic aside. The same unit cites On Temperaments (περὶ κράσεων) for the signs of temperament.

title: Galen faults the author for two ages instead of four
summary: The author divides life into only two ages. Galen holds there should be four, matching the four temperaments: children moist and hot, those in their prime dry and hot, those past their prime dry and cold, the old moist and cold.
quote: calling that of children moist and hot, that of those in their prime dry and hot, that of those past their prime dry and cold, and that of the old moist and cold.
note: He puts the best temperament between childhood and prime (youths and lads, K15.186-187).

title: Clean clothes in winter, oil-soaked in summer: Galen objects
summary: The author says to wear clean garments in winter and oil-soaked ones in summer. Galen disagrees: worn, dense-weave clean clothes cool better; oily clothes are dirty, no clean person tolerates them in summer, and they warm in time.
quote: For the oil-soaked ones are in every case dirty, and no cleanly person tolerates dirty garments, especially in summer.
note: Detail on clothing and hygiene.

title: Slimming regimen: exercise fasting, eat while panting, sesame
summary: To grow thin, do all exertion on an empty stomach, eat while still panting and not yet cooled down after a little mixed, not very cold wine, and season dishes with sesame and spices so that fatty food fills quickly.
quote: Fat persons, and all who wish to become thin, must perform all their exertions while fasting, and set about their food while still panting and not yet cooled down
note: Galen warns this has caused liver obstructions in many (K15.193-194).

title: Galen: water before wine after exercise, as athletes do
summary: Galen says wine should not be drunk straight after exercise or the bath, because it goes to the head. Water comes first, as athletes have learned from experience, and cold water should follow warm.
quote: one does not at all deem it right to drink wine immediately after exercises, but water first, just as the athletes too do these things, having been taught by experience.
note: Galen cites his own treatise on hygiene for the distinctions.

title: Suspected copyist error: 'not very cold' wine
summary: Galen thinks the text bidding 'not very cold' wine may be a copyist's error, since cold wine tightens the body and the author wants to relax it. The draft's account of the intended correction ('not at all hot' / 'not too cold') is confused.
quote: Perhaps, then, it was written otherwise, and the one who copied it erred; for many such things are seen happening even now
note: The Greek reads δέον ἀντὶ τοῦ μήθ᾿ ὅλως θερμὸν αὐτὸν γράψαι, μὴ λίαν ψυχρόν; which of the two phrases is the transmitted reading and which the proposed one is ambiguous, and the draft's order may be inverted. The next sentence, on very hot wine also tightening the stomach, needs checking against this.

title: Slimming: one meal, no bath, hard bed, walk naked
summary: The fat should eat once a day, skip bathing, sleep on a hard bed and walk about naked as far as possible. Galen would rather say 'eat little', since some who eat once a day eat more than those who eat twice.
quote: But also to eat once a day, and to go unbathed, and to sleep on a hard bed, and to walk about naked, as far as may be at all possible.
note: The opposite regimen fattens: two baths, food two or three times a day, a soft bed (K15.196-197).

title: Trainers' 'body-fighting' exercises to build flesh
summary: Trainers fatten clients with grappling exercises they call 'body-fighting', and avoid exercising them naked or without grappling. Those they want thin get fast exercise without the initial grappling.
quote: For this reason, at any rate, the trainers also include the exercises performed with laying hold of one another and 'body-fighting' (σωματομαχεῖν)
note: Gymnastic jargon.

title: Vomiting in the six winter months, enemas in summer
summary: Use vomiting during the six winter months, which are more phlegmatic, and enemas ('washings-out') in hot weather, when the body is more bilious. Purging drugs are different, acting on the whole body.
quote: to vomit during the six winter months; for this time is more phlegmatic than the summer one, and the diseases arise about the head and about this region above the diaphragm.
note: Per the Aphorisms, purge upward in summer and downward in winter (K15.198-199).

title: Enema materials: milk, chickpea water, brine, sea-water
summary: Oily, thick enemas are made from milk or water in which chickpeas were boiled, and suit the thin, who are more bilious. Thin, salty ones of brine or sea-water are more cutting and suit the fat, who are more phlegmatic.
quote: Among the clysters, the oily and thick ones are those made from milks and boiled chickpea-water and [200] the other things of that kind; the thin and salty ones are brine and sea-water and the like.

title: Hyssop emetic for the fat
summary: The fat should vomit fasting, around midday, after running or walking fast. They drink half a kotyle of pounded hyssop in a chous of water, with vinegar and salt to taste, slowly at first and then faster.
quote: Let there be a half-kotyle of pounded hyssop in a chous of water, and let him drink this off, pouring in vinegar and adding salt, in whatever way it is likely to be most pleasant.
note: Galen explains the cutting drink as suited to the thick, cold humours of fat people.

title: The chous varies by place; Galen finds the Attic chous too much
summary: Galen cannot fix the quantity, because the chous is not the same size everywhere. If the Attic chous is meant, he thinks it too much, though the ancients gave whey and washing-out drinks in very large amounts.
quote: But if he orders one to drink the Attic chous, I do not altogether agree
note: Evidence on regional variation in ancient measures (K15.200-201).

title: Emetic for the thin: warm bath, mixed foods, three wines
summary: The thin vomit after food. Bathe in warm water, drink a kotyle of unmixed wine, eat many kinds of food, wait as long as it takes to walk four stades, then drink three wines (austere, sweet, sour), first strong and slow, then watery, fast and plentiful.
quote: let them hold off for as long as it takes to traverse four stades. Then, having mixed together three wines, give them to drink, an austere, a sweet and a sour one
note: Time measured as a walking distance.

title: Dogmatists issue precepts like royal commands
summary: Galen repeats to his companions and friends that dogmatist physicians err by giving orders without reasons, like royal decrees. Hippocrates did better in giving the properties of ptisan.
quote: The men who champion the dogmatic sect seem to me to err in no small way when, without stating the reasoning behind what they recommend, they issue pronouncements as if they were royal commands.
note: Quotes Regimen in Acute Diseases on ptisan's viscous part as smooth and soothing.

title: Infants: long warm baths and very watery wine
summary: Babies should be bathed in warm water for a long time and given very watery wine that is not cold and does not cause wind, so that they have fewer convulsions, grow larger and have a better colour.
quote: Infant children should be bathed in warm water for a long time, and should be given wine to drink that is most watery and not altogether cold
note: Galen: tense bodies are more prone to spasm (citing Hippocrates), and infants are prone because of weak nerves and greedy eating.

title: Galen rejects drying regimen for women
summary: The author prescribes a drier regimen for women, for their soft flesh and for the womb and embryo. Galen objects that women's moistness is natural and should be preserved unless it goes beyond healthy proportion.
quote: but since this is in accordance with nature for them, one ought to preserve it, except if it should at some point exceed the healthy due proportion.

title: Athletes with diarrhoea: cut exercise by a third, halve food
summary: Athletes who get diarrhoea with undigested stools should cut their exercise by at least a third and halve their food, eating very well-baked bread crumbled into wine, with little strong drink, one meal, and no walk after it.
quote: Let the food for these be bread as thoroughly baked as possible, crumbled into wine, and let the drinks be as small as possible and as unmixed as possible
note: The author blames dense flesh and forced meat-eating (K15.213-214); Galen would treat the cause with gentle rubbing and much oil in the bath.

title: Commentaries on the Aphorisms: athletes' peak condition is precarious
summary: Galen recalls showing in his Aphorisms commentaries that athletes' peak condition, full of blood and flesh, is precarious. In dense-fleshed bodies it comes and goes quickly.
quote: For it was shown in the commentaries on the Aphorisms that the good condition of athletes, along with repletion of blood and of flesh, is one that preserves the strength of the natural faculties.
note: The unit's checks failed. The draft's 'preserves the strength' may misread the Greek; Aph. I.3 is about extreme good condition being dangerous.

title: Liver pain after exercise or bathing after meals
summary: In people without fever, exercising or bathing after a meal causes pain in the viscera, especially the liver, from thick humours blocking the narrow vessel ends. They should rest and take diuretics that open the liver, or growths and fevers follow.
quote: Such people must rest during the time in which they are in pain, and drink some one of the remedies that are diuretic and that unblock the liver.
note: A physiological account of blood passing from the concave to the convex parts of the liver.

title: Brain-disease and strangury passage suspected spurious
summary: A passage on brain diseases with numbness and strangury, ending when water or mucus breaks out of the nose or ears, has rightly been suspected. Some reject it as neither Polybus' nor Hippocrates', and Galen agrees its claims are untrue.
quote: With good reason people have regarded this passage with suspicion, and some have even condemned it outright, on the grounds that neither Polybus wrote it, nor, still less, Hippocrates.
note: The passage (K15.221-222) describes nine days of strangury and sight being 'stolen' afterwards.
